extracted.intended_audience: literate London coffee-house readers; general readership interested in manners, satire, and literary criticism (early-18th-century periodical audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted material is from Tatler-style periodical essays discussing social customs, duelling etiquette, literary taste, and public manners; useful for analyzing norms and argumentative style in early-18th-century journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of seconds in duels
rubrics_metrics.description: Seconds ... were to see that all was upon the square, and make a faithful report of the whole combat; but in a little time it became a fashion for the seconds to fight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally the second's duty was impartial oversight and reporting; an anti-pattern developed when seconds began to fight themselves, subverting the oversight role and turning seconds into additional principals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of weapons
rubrics_metrics.description: That's true, sir; for the weapons were always equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dueling custom required equal weapons to avoid unfair advantage; principals even 'put on their pumps, and stripped to their shirts' to show they carried nothing hidden. This is presented as a normative principle to preserve perceived honourable fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pistols when skill imbalance exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose an active, adroit, strong man, had insulted an awkward, or a feeble, or an unpractised swordsman. Then, sir, they fought with pistols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pistols were used as the remedy for mismatched swordsmanship, but the essay notes the significant advantage a good marksman has at distance and questions the honour of killing where technical tricks make the outcome secure; also mentions variants like fighting 'upon a cloak with pistols' to mitigate advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yield rule: first man disarmed or killed considered vanquished
rubrics_metrics.description: It was a law among the combatants, that the party which happened to have the first man disarmed or killed, should yield as vanquished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule aimed to limit casualties and determine the victor without prolonged bloodshed; the text notes it could encourage repeated quarrelling by making one side bear the risk, and that perception of burden on 'very topping fellows' caused changes in fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customary acts to show lack of concealed advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: There the principals put on their pumps, and stripped to their shirts, to show they had nothing but what men of honour carry about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical rites (stripping to shirts, matching swords) functioned as rituals ensuring no concealed weaponry or advantage—presented as important evidentiary gestures demonstrating fair play and honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between a lunatic and a fool (legal/guardianship standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lunatic is in the care of the Chancery, but a fool in that of the Crown... Mr. Locke has somewhere made a distinction between a madman and a fool: a fool is he that from right principles makes a wrong conclusion; but a madman is one who draws a just inference from false principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is used to justify different legal custody/guardianship regimes: lunatics handled by Chancery (equity protection), fools by the Crown (to protect estates). The essay uses Locke's characterizations as criteria for differentiating incapacity types with legal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for discerning the taste of an age via comedies
rubrics_metrics.description: There was no method in the world of knowing the taste of an age, or period of time so good, as by the observations of the persons represented in their comedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion proposes that dramatic characters provide reliable evidence of social tastes and manners; examples given compare characterization of women in Shakespeare's time (housewives, mothers) with later periods (virtuosas, coquettes), implying a method for literary-historical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle that fashion governs behaviour (esp. 'very pretty fellows')
rubrics_metrics.description: I am of opinion, Mr. Sage, that fashion governs a very pretty fellow; nature, or common sense, your ordinary persons, and sometimes men of fine parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social conduct and concepts of honour or 'being a very pretty fellow' are presented as largely determined by fashion; this functions as a sociological criterion for explaining collective behaviours such as duelling customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical guideline on battle-report style and its pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: These elegant expressions, 'Ditto,' 'And so,' 'But soon,' 'But having,' 'But could not,' 'But are,' 'But they,' 'Finds the party to have found,' &c., do certainly give great life and spirit to the relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented satirically: while certain repetitive connectives may seem to impart 'life and spirit' to a battle narrative, the essay criticizes clichéd, vague phrasing and lack of identifying details (e.g., unnamed commanders) as faults. Implicit guidance: prefer clear, specific, and well-named actions over formulaic connectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of generous/guardian love (criterion of 'true love')
rubrics_metrics.description: This is that sort of passion which truly deserves the name of 'love,' and has something more generous than friendship itself; for it has a constant care of the object beloved, abstracted from its own interests in the possession of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on Suckling and Milton, the essay identifies 'love' as protective, self-abnegating care—a normative criterion distinguishing true love from mere desire or vanity.
